source: Xu, Martelaro, McComb (2026) Supervising Ralph Wiggum: cost measure re-read
finding: Gap 1 check. The paper matches the three systems on design STEPS, not on tokens. The separate monitor (CRDAL) adds a second agent call on every step, so its token cost is higher than RWL and SRL even though steps are equal.
numbers: Mean steps before final design: RWL 9.07 (SD 7.02), SRL 9.10 (4.45), CRDAL 9.37 (3.20); ANOVA F(2,87)=0.031, p=0.97. Pairwise d between 0.006 and 0.069. Capacity: RWL 72.07 Ah, SRL 106.08, CRDAL 141.17 (30 runs each, one RWL run failed). One task (battery pack), Gemini 3.1 Pro.
limits: Authors use step count as the cost proxy because they assume simulation costs more than LLM calls. No token or dollar figures. One task, one model, no second domain. No replication found.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open. The CRDAL gain is real on one task but is NOT shown at equal total tokens. Any test of our monitor must log tokens for the monitor and compare to a self-reflection loop given the same extra budget.

source: Renze and Guven (2024) Self-reflection in LLM agents: effects on problem-solving performance
finding: Self-reflection helps, but the design reflects only on answers already known to be wrong. Even a bare 'you were wrong, retry' agent with no content gained accuracy.
numbers: 1,000 multiple-choice questions from several exams, nine LLMs, eight reflection types. Reflection was run only on questions the baseline got wrong. All-model table: baseline 0.786; Retry 0.827 (+0.041); Advice 0.840; Explanation 0.876; Solution 0.925; Composite 0.932; Unredacted (answer leaked) 0.971. All p<0.001 (McNemar).
limits: The design counts only re-answers of wrong items, so it adds a free correctness oracle. Solution and Composite types give indirect hints toward the answer. Exam ceiling compresses gains. Not a design task.
agent_relevance: When we compare a monitor against self-reflection, both must get the same validator signal. Part of any 'reflection gain' is just being told the draft failed. Guardrails that fire on a code-checked failure fit this.

source: Bertalanic and Fortuna (2026) The Cost of Consensus: isolated self-correction vs homogeneous multi-agent debate
finding: A second agent of the same model is not a better checker. Unguided peer debate among identical small models did no better, and often worse, than one agent correcting itself, at 2.1 to 3.4 times the tokens.
numbers: Teams of 10 homogeneous agents (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Ministral-3-8B), 3 rounds, GSM-Hard and MMLU-Hard, N=100 problems per cell (1017 for Qwen on GSM-Hard). Ministral GSM-Hard: base 24.7%, debate 20.7%, self-correction 48.3% (p<0.001). Ministral MMLU-Hard: debate 62.0% vs self 65.3% (p=0.002). Llama MMLU-Hard: debate 45.0% vs self 47.7% (p=0.131, n.s.). Tokens per problem: debate 17.4k to 28.6k vs self 5.3k to 12.8k. Vulnerability rate (correct answers destroyed by peer logic) 70.0% for Ministral on GSM-Hard.
limits: Peer debate, not a role-specialised monitor with different instructions. Small 7-8B models, maths and MMLU, no design task. Some p-values uncorrected.
agent_relevance: A monitor only helps if it differs from the actor (different role, different information, or a code check). Same-model peers add cost and conformity. Supports code checks over more LLM voices.

source: Revisiting Multi-Agent Debate as test-time scaling: a systematic study of conditional effectiveness (2025)
finding: At an equal budget of 16 generations, parallel self-consistency beat sequential refinement and debate on maths. Debate only caught up on the hardest problems and with weak models. Agent diversity added little.
numbers: Budget fixed at 16 generations per problem: SC 16 samples, SR 16 rounds, MAD 2x8, 4x4, 8x2. MATH500 / AIME: Qwen2.5-7B SC 81.3 / 15.6, SR 71.5 / 11.1, MAD 4x4 78.1 / 14.4. Qwen2.5-32B SC 84.0 / 20.6, SR 81.9 / 11.1. Qwen2.5-3B AIME: SC 8.9, MAD 4x4 11.1, MAD 8x2 10.0 (paper says MAD doubles AIME accuracy for this model). Closed models: SC best (GPT-4o 79.8 / 16.7, SR 75.1 / 3.3); closed models run once.
limits: Maths and safety tasks only. Not a metacognitive monitor, but it is the nearest equal-budget comparison of one-agent loops against multi-agent loops.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly answered for maths: at equal generations the cheap parallel restart beats the loop. Our plan should keep plain best-of-N as the control arm for any monitor.

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix: full Table 8 and Table 9 re-read for the one-line constraint question
finding: Gap 3. A short 'go beyond obvious answers, include wild directions' prompt (the AI-specific family) beat the control prompts on novelty, diversity and rarity by large margins. TRIZ matched it on novelty. C-K, Design Thinking and SCAMPER often did not beat control. Method prompts also cut the number of ideas listed.
numbers: 25 prompts, 5 models, three runs. t-test p vs control, novelty: AI-specific 1.16e-34, TRIZ 2.24e-44, Design Thinking 2.16e-2, Scenario 1.18e-2, C-K 1.04e-1 (n.s.), SCAMPER 2.81e-1 (n.s.), Brainstorming 8.18e-2 (n.s.). Diversity p: AI-specific 1.11e-124, Brainstorming 7.27e-38, C-K 1.32e-45, TRIZ 1.94e-1 (n.s.). Fluency (ideas per list) in Table 8: control 19 to 24; C-K about 10 to 11; TRIZ 9 to 12; AI-specific alt 2 and 3 about 24. Top-5 novelty gain vs control: TRIZ +35.62%, C-K +40.31%.
quote: simpler prompts emphasizing such cues tend to outperform more complex, method-based prompts
limits: Equal TOKENS not enforced: max 8192 tokens for all, but method prompts are longer and yield fewer ideas, so novelty per list is confounded with list length and with a novelty metric defined against the control set. Huge p-values come from many pooled items, not independent briefs. Metrics are embedding-based, no human raters.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 mostly closed: a short avoid-the-obvious cue is at least as good as long method scripts for novelty and diversity. Use it as the cheap baseline arm; claim method scaffolds only if they beat it at equal tokens.

source: Rosenbaum et al. (2025) divergent and convergent personas: what was measured
finding: Gap 5 check. The divergent-helps, convergent-does-not result is about self-rated creativity enhancement by humans, not output quality, and the human chose which persona to use.
numbers: Divergent persona 'Taylor' rated higher than control, difference +0.89 (g=0.69, p=.003). Convergent persona 'Alex': treatment 2.70 (SD 1.23) vs control 2.76 (SD 1.38), p=.837. Forced choice: treatment 78.8% credited the divergent persona (52% rated 1, 27% rated 2). Control group favoured the convergent persona (t(28)=3.55, p=.0013). Conscientiousness and neuroticism steered users to the convergent persona.
limits: Self-report ratings, about 105 recruited, two personas in one tool. No agent-only condition, no blind rating of output quality.
agent_relevance: Cannot conclude that convergent scaffolds are useless: control users already leaned convergent. For an agent with no human, test diverge then converge stages against output quality.

source: Nguyen, Tschiatschek, Singla (2025) Enhancing diversity of LLM-generated educational tasks (CreativeDC, divergent-convergent prompting)
finding: Gap 5, agent-only. A two-stage prompt (stage 1 diverge on the theme, stage 2 converge on constraints) gave about 1.6 times more distinct good tasks than plain or step-by-step prompting, with no human in the loop.
numbers: Qwen3-235B-A22B, temperature 1.0, Python programming tasks. At K=50 tasks: CreativeDC about 12 distinct high-utility tasks (13 over all tasks) vs about 8 for BASE and COT (paired Wilcoxon p<0.001, Bonferroni). BASE and COT not different. Experts (3): about 16 clusters vs 9 for COT. Novelty win rate 96.67% (SE 2.32), interestingness 0.81 vs 0.50; task validity 1.00 vs 0.78.
limits: Three expert raters, one concept ('Variables'), 20 pairs for the novelty test. No divergent-only or convergent-only ablation, so it cannot say which stage did the work. Education tasks, not design. Token cost of the two-stage prompt not matched.
agent_relevance: Supports a diverge-then-converge operator order for an agent alone. Next test: ablate each stage and match tokens against best-of-N.

source: Chen, Zhao, Cohan (2026) Measuring the gap between human and LLM research ideas
finding: Gap 6. LLMs alone frame research gaps in a narrow way. Their ideas pile up on 'bridge two things' and 'synthesis' framings, far more than human papers do.
numbers: Nine main LLMs given the prior works behind a paper. Human ideas: 12.1% bridge or fragmentation opportunities, 5.1% synthesis method. LLM ideas: 47.1% to 64.2% bridge, 22.5% to 38.7% synthesis. Thinking mode raised bridge share (one model 49.7% to 71.1%) and synthesis (38.7% to 52.2%). Taxonomy validated on 150 held-out papers.
limits: Research ideas, not design briefs. Labels made by an LLM annotator. Describes the gap; does not test a reframing operator.
agent_relevance: A reframe operator that simply asks again will probably return the same bridge framing. Force different framing types and count framing-type spread, not only novelty.

source: Gao et al. (2026) RE-SEARCH: dissecting LLM ideation through a two-player questioning game
finding: Gap 6. Models can judge a good question or idea but cannot produce it. Most progress happens in the first 30 of 100 questions. Failing runs either over-exploit one direction or over-explore.
numbers: 200 ICML 2026 papers, three games per paper, six LLMs. Weak model picking from a four-model pool of candidate questions: scores 5.19 to 5.34; gain over solo +1.04 (GPT-OSS-120B), +1.09 (Qwen3.6-35B), +1.07 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash); GPT-5.4 -0.59. Self best-of-4 only 4.16 to 4.57; random pick from the pool 4.43. Knowing the idea explains barely 10% of the model gap. Over-exploring traces 13.7 top-level branches, balanced 7.2 to 8.2, over-exploiting 5.2 to 5.5.
limits: Research-idea rediscovery with a yes/no oracle, LLM-judged idea cards (judges agree at 0.85 to 0.88). Not design.
agent_relevance: Generation, not judgment, is the bottleneck: an agent should import outside candidate framings (other models, a survey of options) and keep its own checking for selection.

source: Gao et al. (2026) RE-SEARCH: survey of the hypothesis space as external input
finding: Same paper. Handing the model an overview of the hypothesis space (five to seven dimensions, four to six approaches each) lifted weak models most. Naming the true idea mattered more than a decoy.
numbers: Survey lists 20 to 42 candidates. Full survey raised final score by up to 1.25 points, largest for the lowest scorers (r=-0.74). Models ask about the named idea within a median of 3 to 6 questions; named idea asked in 67% to 89% of games vs 29% to 52% under a decoy.
limits: The survey included the true idea in the main condition, so it is an upper bound. Decoy and dummy conditions show part of the gain is real structure.
agent_relevance: A typed map of the option space (dimension by approach) is a cheap input to the divergence step. It is a measured analogue of idea fragments, though not an agent memory.

source: Mizrahi et al. (2025) Cooking Up Creativity: structured recombination (Dish COVER)
finding: Gap 8 analogue. Parsing ideas into typed trees, recombining them with code, then writing back to text produced more novel recipes than GPT-4o prompted many ways. No agent memory was tested.
numbers: GPT-4o baseline built from pools of 104 (Exp 1) and 114 (Exp 2) prompt paraphrases, temperature 1. Exp 1 (10 dish pairs, 50 recipes per model): novelty 3.53 vs 3.146 (p=0.0009). Exp 2 (100 recipes each): 3.612 vs 3.141 (p=9.2e-8). Within-model similarity 0.387 vs 0.659 (Exp 1), 0.402 vs 0.731 (Exp 2). Nearest known recipe similarity 0.774 vs 0.851. Valuable: 80% vs 82% (Exp 1), 85% vs 98% (Exp 2).
limits: Cooking domain, cooking-expert ratings. The structure is a recipe tree, not what/how/value fragments. Value fell in Exp 2. The advantage comes from external code operations, not from the memory format.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for typed fragments as agent memory. Weak evidence says: let code do the recombination of typed pieces, and keep a value check.

source: Huang et al. (2025, v2 2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLMs with synthetic data (SynAnchors)
finding: Gap 4 analogue. LLMs themselves are anchored by the first number or option they see. Conventional prompt fixes do not remove it. Reasoning models are least affected.
numbers: Share of questions anchored: 22% to 61% across models. Examples: Qwen2.5-7B 43.3%, GPT-4o 48.3%, GPT-4o-mini 38.3%, DeepSeek-R1 36.7% (DeepThink row). Mechanism analysis: the anchor effect sits in shallow layers; reasoning traces mention the anchor less as they lengthen.
limits: Numeric and semantic estimation, not design examples. Mitigations tested on two models only.
agent_relevance: Supports a guardrail that withholds or delays the first example, and long reasoning before answering. Does not give a design-fixation effect size.

source: Anon (2024, revised 2025) How AI ideas affect the creativity, diversity and evolution of human ideas
finding: Gap 4 analogue (human side). Seeing many ChatGPT example ideas did not change individual creativity, but made the group's ideas more spread out. Seeing few AI examples did nothing.
numbers: 800+ participants, 40+ countries; Alternate Uses Task; high exposure (4 AI plus 2 human examples) vs low (2 AI plus 4 human); disclosure yes or no, no main effect of disclosure. High exposure: collective diversity up and rising faster; individual creativity unchanged. The paper says AI made ideas different, not better.
limits: Examples were AI ideas or earlier participants' ideas; diversity measured as embedding distance. Brief task, one session. First author names not checked.
agent_relevance: Examples can widen the pool without raising quality. This sits beside Wadinambiarachchi 2024 (anchoring, N=60). The difference is group diversity vs individual copying, so measure both.

source: Mokryn, Ayalon, Dines, Shaer (2026) AI as Anchor: interview sequencing and synthetic stakeholder voices in design education
finding: Order of use changes how an AI source is used. When the AI stakeholder came first it gave a broad, general frame that students later revised; when it came after human interviews it was used to check findings. Final designs followed human-derived concerns more.
numbers: 8 teams (N=21; 19 undergraduate, 2 graduate), one semester, GPT-4o simulated stakeholders. Final-design correspondence: 39 of 43 prominent human-derived pain points (90.7%) vs 22 of 32 AI-derived (68.8%). 13 written reflections, 3 post-course participants (14.3%).
limits: Exploratory field study, qualitative, not randomised, overlapping rates are not independent tests. Novice students.
agent_relevance: A cheap real-world measure of anchoring by AI input order. Test in an agent: reorder 'AI frame first' vs 'evidence first' and count which concerns survive to the final design.

source: Rusia, Bhole, Gupta, Dey (2026) Design Creativity Bench: measuring creativity in LLM-generated UI
finding: Out-of-the-box LLM design output is appropriate but repetitive. Models are more alike than human designers are.
numbers: 15 models, 80 tasks, 80 differentiated brief pairs per model. Originality (distance between designs from different models, same prompt): 0.592 (95% CI 0.582 to 0.602) vs 0.764 for human vs model pairs. Creative range across models 0.581 vs 0.902 for humans. Appropriateness above 90% for every model, best 99.2%, humans 98.0%.
limits: UI HTML designs, default temperature and sampling; human designers could use Behance and a gallery. Distances are embedding-based. No intervention tested.
agent_relevance: Quality is not the problem, spread is. Scaffolds should be scored on spread across restarts as well as on single outputs.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001; reprinted Cross 2024 ch. 5) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution
finding: Gap 7. The reprint abstract confirms the base: protocol studies of nine experienced industrial designers on one realistic task, concept quality rated by a panel of educators. The co-evolution model was confirmed in general, but the authors add that in creative design the solution space may be structured BEFORE the problem space, using precedents.
numbers: N=9 designers, one design task. Chapter page gave the abstract only, not the full text or tables.
quote: structuring the solution space prior to the problem space
limits: Per-designer ratings and episode counts not read. Small N. Solution-first can precede problem framing, so Cross 1982's 'solution-first' is a style, not a rule.
agent_relevance: The designerly loop is two-way. Do not hard-code problem-first or solution-first; use whichever signal says one space is thin. Gap 7 partly closed (N=9 confirmed); Lawson 1979 numbers still not obtained.

source: Cross (1999; reprinted 2024 ch. 7) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies
finding: Gap 9. Cross's own cross-domain review lists solution focusing, co-evolution, fixation, opportunism and expert-novice differences from protocol studies and says similarities across domains are many. It is a self-review. No independent replication or critique of the five aspects came up.
numbers: Abstract and reference list read. References include Lawson 1979 (Ergonomics 22(1)), Lawson 1994, Lloyd and Scott 1994 and 1995, Lloyd, Lawson and Scott 1996. No numbers.
limits: Author reviewing own programme. Page showed only abstract and references.
agent_relevance: No independent test of the five aspects found. Treat them as design hypotheses, not facts, for the schema.

source: Sio, Kotovsky, Cagan (2015) Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes
finding: Gap 4. The record exists (Crossref lists it, Design Studies, July 2015). Full text is paywalled: ScienceDirect returned 403, ResearchGate 403, Semantic Scholar 429. Effect sizes were not obtained.
limits: Not opened. A 2018 review (SHS Web of Conferences 48, 01061; abstract only via Crossref) says example effects depend on quantity, abstraction and proximity of examples.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. Until read, treat 'examples fixate' as conditional on example type, not a constant effect.

source: Failure to find: LLM test of Lawson's block puzzle or solution-first behaviour
finding: Gap 2. Paper search (Hugging Face paper search; arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited) for 'Lawson block puzzle problem-focused solution-focused', and for problem-solution co-evolution with LLM agents, returned grid-puzzle benchmarks and software-agent papers. None tests Lawson's task.
numbers: 0 relevant hits in 2 queries. Nearest evidence: Zhang 2025 (GPT-4o runs sustain focus on one space, c03) and Re-Search over-exploit and over-explore (d09).
limits: Absence under a rate-limited semantic search is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. It is a cheap original test: give an LLM a Lawson-style hidden-rule puzzle with and without a forced 'explore the rule first' step and compare solve counts at equal tokens.
